
# The project hierarchy

Think of the project like this:

```
Project
│
├── Gradle (build system)
│
├── AndroidManifest.xml
│
├── Kotlin source
│     ├── Activities
│     ├── ViewModels
│     ├── UI
│     ├── Data
│     └── Services
│
└── Resources

```

 **`app/build/`:** is generated by Gradle every time you build. Never edit anything there.

---

# 1. Build system (learn these first)

```
build.gradle.kts
app/build.gradle.kts
settings.gradle.kts
gradle.properties
```

These files describe the project.

For example

```
app/build.gradle.kts
```

contains things like

* Kotlin version
* Android SDK version
* libraries
* Compose
* dependencies
* compiler options

Whenever something won't compile...

...this is usually where the problem starts.

---

# 2. AndroidManifest.xml

```
app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
```

This is the heart of the Android app.

It tells Android

* what the app is
* what permissions it needs
* what services exist
* what Activity starts first

You'll eventually memorize it.

---

# 3. Kotlin code

This is where almost all learning happens.

```
src/main/kotlin/com/example/messageintelligence
```

contains

```
MainActivity.kt
MainViewModel.kt

data/
service/
ui/
```

Think of it as

```
Activity
      ↓
ViewModel
      ↓
Repository
      ↓
Data
```


---

# Learn these in this order

## 1.

```
MainActivity.kt
```

This is the app entry point.

It usually looks like

```kotlin
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(...) {

        setContent {

        }

    }

}
```

Learn

* classes
* inheritance
* override
* functions
* lifecycle

---

## 2.

```
MessageIntelligenceApp.kt
```

This is the Compose UI.

You'll learn

```
@Composable

Column()

Row()

Text()

Button()

LazyColumn()
```

Most Kotlin beginners spend a lot of time here.

---

## 3.

```
MainViewModel.kt
```

Probably the single most educational file.

It teaches

* classes
* mutable state
* functions
* data flow

Typical flow

```
Button clicked

↓

ViewModel changes state

↓

Compose redraws UI
```

---

## 4.

```
MessageRepository.kt
```

Repositories manage data.

You'll learn

```
List<Message>

filter()

map()

sorted()

when

if

loops
```

This file is usually "pure Kotlin."

---

## 5.

```
MessageProcessor.kt
```

Usually contains business logic.

Good place to learn

```
when

if

functions

String

Regex

collections
```

---

## 6.

```
MessageData.kt
```

Probably contains

```kotlin
data class Message(...)
```

This teaches

```
data class

properties

constructors

copy()

equals()
```

Every Kotlin programmer uses data classes constantly.

---

# Services

```
service/

MessageNotificationListener.kt

UiInspectionAccessibilityService.kt
```

These are Android-specific.

Read them later.

They teach

```
inheritance

override

callbacks

notifications

Accessibility APIs
```

---

# Theme

```
ui/theme
```

```
Color.kt

Theme.kt

Type.kt
```

Mostly UI styling.

Good to know.

Not essential initially.

---

# Resources

```
res/
```

Contains

```
strings.xml

colors.xml

themes.xml

drawable/

xml/
```

Unlike Kotlin,

these are XML.

Android still uses XML for many things.

---

# Ignore these

Don't waste time here.

```
build/

outputs/

tmp/

intermediates/

generated/

kotlin/

dex/

classes/

```

Those are generated by Gradle.

Think of them as

```
.c files

.o files

.exe
```

from C programming.

# Running the project without IntelliJ

Everything IntelliJ does can be done from the terminal.

Build:

```bash
./gradlew build
```

Build debug APK:

```bash
./gradlew assembleDebug
```

Clean:

```bash
./gradlew clean
```

Install on a connected device/emulator:

```bash
adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
```

Run unit tests:

```bash
./gradlew test
```

Run Android instrumentation tests (requires a device or emulator):

```bash
./gradlew connectedAndroidTest
```

See available Gradle tasks:

```bash
./gradlew tasks
```

Get more detailed build output for debugging:

```bash
./gradlew assembleDebug --info
```

or

```bash
./gradlew assembleDebug --stacktrace
```

---

# Debugging without IntelliJ

Since you're working from Kali/Linux and not using IntelliJ, your main tools are:

* `adb logcat` — view application logs and crashes in real time.
* `println()` — quick console output during development (less common on Android).
* `android.util.Log`:

  ```kotlin
  Log.d("MainViewModel", "Message received: $message")
  ```

  Then filter with:

  ```bash
  adb logcat | grep MainViewModel
  ```
* `adb shell` — interact with the device or emulator.
* `jadx` or `apktool` (if you're curious about generated APK contents after building).

---

# Your project as an MVC/MVVM map

Based on the files you've shown, here's the architecture:

```
MainActivity.kt
        │
        ▼
MessageIntelligenceApp.kt
        │
        ▼
MainViewModel.kt
        │
        ▼
MessageRepository.kt
        │
        ▼
MessageProcessor.kt
        │
        ▼
MessageData.kt
```

Alongside this, the Android system can invoke:

```
MessageNotificationListener.kt
                │
                ▼
         MainViewModel / Repository

UiInspectionAccessibilityService.kt
                │
                ▼
         MainViewModel / Repository
```

This is a clean **MVVM (Model–View–ViewModel)** structure, and understanding how data flows through these files will teach you not only Kotlin syntax but also how a modern Android application is organized.

If you're learning by reading and modifying code, I'd recommend focusing on **one file at a time**. Start with `MainActivity.kt`, trace every function call into `MessageIntelligenceApp.kt`, then into `MainViewModel.kt`, and only then move into the `data` package. That mirrors how the app actually executes and makes the codebase much easier to understand.
